header.author: Augustine, Saint
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's stoa0040.stoa080b.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa080b.opp-l: The edition is badly scanned; evident readings have been translated (e.g. sapidam for saporam, adaugens for adaugen, medullis for medallis, da for na, sumus caeli for snmuscocli, unde for nude, tuae for luae, vitia for vilia). Line 1: a stray 'dedisti' after 'charitas' is omitted; 'tulta' read as 'ablata/sublata'; text is lost after 'matris Ec[clesiae]', where a word or line has dropped; 'evaneo' is duplicated. Line 3 is seriously damaged: the chapter heading and the opening of the chapter (presumably 'God is spirit', John 4:24) are lost in garble; the passage follows Augustine, Confessions 1.2–3, and words lost at 'Cur itaque peto ut... enim ego jam sum inferi' and 'te totum capere omnia' are supplied in brackets from that sense; 'quoniam quae te plena sunt' is rendered with the Confessions' fuller sense, which the scan appears to have shortened. Line 4 quotes Boethius, Consolation 3 m.9 ('da... sedem... defigere visus', 'Dissice terrenae nebulas...').

Ch. IV: "Reditis debita" read as "Reddis debita". Ch. VI title "moretur" probably for "movetur"; translated so. Ch. X: "ab ipso lunc avo" read as "ab aevo" (Boethius, Cons. III m.9). Ch. XI: "sed ero" read as "sed ego".

Line 13: 'passionum indigna' is obscure (perhaps 'unworthy [terms] of passions'); rendered literally. Line 14: 'ad efficientias causarum' uncertain; rendered as 'for the bringing about of [your] purposes'. Line 16: 'hand recte' read as 'hanc rectae'; 'Legislatorum filii' presumably the Jews. 'Priusquam creaturae ostenderes creatorem' may mean 'before you showed the Creator [in the form of] a creature', i.e. the Incarnation. Line 17: 'Verbum quomodo ili Patre' read as 'in Patre'.

Line 19: 'sommæ' read as 'summæ'. Line 23: the scanned 'api'In' is read as 'sapiam'. The biblical reference printed as Ps. 133:16 corresponds to Ps. 138:16 (Vulgate), 'imperfectum meum viderunt oculi tui'. Line 24: the closing sentence ('non enim summae bonitatis ... profitemur originem ...; sed ejus participatione dicimus bona omnia') is awkward as printed and may be corrupt. The sense seems to be that the supreme goodness is professed as the origin of all things, and that other things are called good by participation in it; the bracketed words supply this reading.

Several scanning errors corrected silently. In ch. XXV 'inertum' read as 'insertum' (inserted), and 'non 2 confusum' as 'nihil confusum'. In ch. XXVII 'in Pater diccris' read as 'tu Pater diceris'; 'impatefactam' taken as 'not yet laid open'. In ch. XXVIII 'species' and 'forma' are near-synonyms (beauty/form), rendered to keep the wordplay of 'speciosissimum' and 'formosissimum'. The scriptural citation 'Psal. CXXXIII, 16' in the preceding stretch refers to Ps. 138:16 (Vulgate).

33: 'videm' read as 'videbunt'; 'vides t' read as 'vides te'. 34: the opening is garbled ('inter Scyllam integra et Charybdim ita tenere iter per mercibus'), apparently with words displaced from the next clause; translated as 'between Scylla and Charybdis so to hold our course'. 'te incircumscriptum afficitur' seems corrupt; a verb such as 'aspicit' (beholds) is supplied. 'bonorum insinuator' is obscure; taken as an address to God, 'you who instil what is good'. 36: 'Sed quia longe distas Creator a non caperis in loco? Omnino enim in loco' is corrupt; translated as if it read 'a creatura' and 'omnino non in loco'. 37: chapter numbered XXIII in the text, evidently for XXXIII. 'recto incedit tramite dominatur vel ordine' is disordered; taken as 'walks the right path or rules in right order'. 'promior' read as 'pronior' (more prone).

Several scanning errors read as evident: 'tucum' as 'tecum'; 'easus' as 'casus'; 'sancturum' as 'sanctum'. 'Ignosce, aviditate pie' is taken as 'Ignosce, pie', with 'aviditate' a dittography from the next clause. 'in medio ideo laqueorum positi, et gemus' is read as 'in medio laqueorum positi, et ideo egemus'. The stray '(a)' is an editorial mark and is omitted. 'nec necessitudo corrumpit' is rendered as if 'necessitas', meaning 'necessity'. 'quia non temeritate' is construed as 'for it was not…'.

nodes.text: THE MIRROR. ONE BOOK.

CHAPTER ONE. Invocation to the Holy Trinity. Be present to me, true light, God the Father almighty. Be present to me, true light from light, the Word, Son of God, God almighty. Be present to me, true illumination, Holy Spirit, unity, holiness and love of the Father and the Son, God almighty. Be present to me, O one Trinity and threefold unity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, one God almighty. My faith calls upon you, Lord, the faith which you gave me through your goodness for my salvation. My chaste conscience calls upon you, my God, and the sweet love of my faith, which you led, once the darkness of ignorance was shaken off, to the understanding of truth; which, once the bitterness of the world was taken away and the sweetness of your love applied, you made savoury and honey-sweet to me. The clear voice and sincere cry of my faith calls upon you, blessed Trinity, the faith which you enlightened, nourishing it in me from the very cradle, which you always [strengthened] by the inspiration of your grace; which, increasing it, you strengthened in me through the ministry of the preaching of mother Church [...]; how sweetly it tastes on the very palate of my soul's joys, how strongly, how often it beats upon my mind, and admonishes it, moving all my senses and the inward parts of my spirit, so that it delights [me] to praise you, because you made us to praise you! But my mind is restless until, gathering itself back from the dispersal by which I am torn to pieces while, turned away from you, the One, I vanish into many things; so that, turned back into myself, and rising above myself, and passing beyond all things and reaching you, I may exult to you with the jubilation of the heart, and bring forth praises by the service of the mouth, so that in meditating on the confession of your glory my heart may grow warm, and my spirit may gape for you, and my mind may burn in your love, forgetful of vanity and misery, while it attends to you alone, and while, astonished and amazed, it clings to the unchangeableness of your glory, and with the eyes of faith beholds you, the sun of justice, as it is written: He who clings to God is one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17).

Therefore I will flee, Lord, and gladly will I flee the clamouring tumults of all vanities. But where shall I flee, to avoid them, to trample them underfoot, and drive them far from the serenity of joyful contemplation? To you, who are the only refuge and the sole hope of the wretched; to you, my glory and the one who lifts up my head (Ps. 3:4); to you I will flee from the pit of misery and the mire of filth (Ps. 39:3). Let me cling to you, as you yourself grant, honey-sweet delight, so that you may grow sweet to me, a sweetness not deceitful, a sweetness happy and secure. Let me seek you, then, Lord, calling upon you, and I will call upon you believing in you; so that seeking you I may find you, and finding you I may bless you, who have blessed us with every blessing. My God, my only hope, hear me: may I not, wearied, be unwilling to seek you, but may I seek your face always and ardently. Give the strength to seek, you who have caused yourself to be found, and have given the hope of finding you more and more. Enlighten, Lord, the eye of my heart with the clear light of inward vision: for it is veiled and blind with the foul darkness of sins and ignorance. Enlighten it with the light of your grace, so that with the sincere eyes of faith and the pure light of the heart I may look into the mysteries of your kingdom. But since praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner (Ecclus. 15:9), and faith without worthy works is not praised, I ask the Father through the Son, I ask the Son through the Father, I ask the Holy Spirit through the Father and the Son, that all vices be removed far from me, and all holy virtues be planted in me: so that the sacrifice of praise of my faith may become acceptable to you, my God, and may ascend to you as a sweet savour. I beseech [you], and as a suppliant I implore your mercy, God, fount and source, giver and preserver of all virtues: increase in me hope, a faith holy, right and spotless, a faith learned, catholic and most prudent, a faith fervent, unconquerable and orthodox; which may work in me, through love and humility, everything that pleases you; which cannot be overcome amid words of dispute, in time of persecution, or in the day of need. God who search hearts and reins (Ps. 7:10), before you are my health and my infirmity: the one, I pray, preserve; the other, heal. Before you are my knowledge and my ignorance. Where you have opened to me, receive me as I enter; where you have shut, open to me as I knock: so that hearing I may understand you, and understanding I may love you, and loving I may praise you, and with my whole heart may desire always to behold the beauty of the vision of you. I hear what your Scripture, which you sanctified and sent into the world, wishes to make known to us; I hear, and I believe it.

CHAPTER II. That God [...] (John 4:24), but a spirit incomprehensible, incorporeal, unchangeable, uncircumscribed, everywhere whole, nowhere divided, according to the truthful testimony of Scripture itself; for in this way you, the Creator, are distinguished from the creature, among which are those also called spirits. If it is so, or rather because it is so, how shall I call upon my God and my Lord? For surely I will call him into myself when I call upon him. And what place is there in me into which my God may come into me, into which he may come who made heaven and earth? Is it so, my God, [is there anything] in me that can contain you? Or do heaven and earth, which you made and in which you made me, contain you? Or, because without you whatever exists would not exist, does it come about that whatever exists contains you? Why then do I ask that [you come into me ...]? For I am already [in] the underworld, and yet you are there: for even if I go down into hell, you are there (Ps. 138:8). So I would not exist, my God, I would not exist at all, unless you were in me. Or rather, I would not exist unless I were in you, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things (Rom. 11:36)? Even so, Lord, even so. Where then do I call you to, since I am in you; or from where would you come into me? For where shall I withdraw, where shall I go? Outside heaven and earth perhaps, so that from there my God may come into me, who said, I fill heaven and earth (Jer. 23:24)? Do heaven and earth then contain you, since you fill them? Or do you fill them, and something remains over, because they do not contain you? And where do you pour out whatever of you remains once heaven and earth are filled? Or have you no need to be contained by anything, you who contain all things, since the things you fill you fill by containing them? For it is not the vessels full of you that make you stable; for even if they are broken, you are not poured out. And when you are poured out upon us, you do not lie low, but raise us up; nor are you scattered, but you gather us. But [as for] you who fill all things, [do you fill them with your whole self? Or, since] all things [cannot] contain you whole, do they contain a part of you, and do all things contain the same part at once? Or does each contain its own, the greater things more, the lesser less? Is some part of you then greater, some lesser? Or are you everywhere whole, and nothing contains you whole? What then are you, Lord my God, what then, but the Lord my God? For who is God but the Lord, or who is God but our God (Ps. 17:32)? Plainly no one, no one. For there is no other besides you, three and one, one and three, neither in heaven above nor on earth below. Who is like you? Who is magnificent in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy in every power, as you are, our God, who do great and wonderful things (Exod. 15:11), and unsearchable things without number? All things magnify you, every spirit praises you, all those hosts of blessed spirits and heavenly citizens adore you and bless you. To you mother Church throughout the whole world offers prayers and unceasingly speaks praises. I, the least of your servants, praise and bless you. Who is like you, Lord (Ps. 88:9)? And rightly all the things you have made obey, serve and tremble before you alone, the Creator; at your nod you do whatever you will.

CHAPTER III. That God made all things by his nod alone, and is whole in all things. For you are truly the only Lord, God invisible, inestimable, uncircumscribed, without place, immeasurable, incomprehensible, everywhere whole, everywhere present, ineffably penetrating all things, containing all things, knowing all things, foreseeing all things, all-powerful, and governing the universe, whole in heaven, whole on earth, whole indeed everywhere; and there is no other besides you, our God, in whom mother Church, apostolic and universal, believes and whom she adores. You are truly to be worshipped and revered, feared and loved with all devotion always, Lord our God. When we did not exist, you made us by your power; and when we were lost by our own fault, you wonderfully recovered us by your mercy and goodness. Therefore I confess to you, king of heaven and earth, and honour you with the sacrifice of praise. And since outward gifts are lacking, with all the inmost parts of the heart that are in me I render vows of praise to you. But since nothing can be offered acceptable to you except from what is yours, you, God, in whose light we see light, give, I beg, light in the heart, give the word in the mouth, grant the mind to ascend to the heavenly seat; grant it to behold the fount of good, grant, the light being found, to fix the clear sight of the soul on you. And since we are partly of heaven, partly of earth, whence the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things (Wis. 9:15); scatter the clouds and the weight of the earthly mass, and illumine with your splendour, I beg, the darkened face of the inner man: halt the wandering minds rushing through many byways. Subject the flesh to the spirit, the appetites to reason, the vices to the virtues, the body to the soul, and subject me inwardly and outwardly in all things to your will: so that, all things being well set in their order, through your grace I may deserve both to love you perfectly and to praise you worthily with lips and heart, crying out to you with all the strength I have, and saying thus:

CHAPTER IV. On the essence of the Godhead. Highest, best, most mighty, most merciful, most just, most hidden, most present, most beautiful, most strong, most sweet, most unconquered, most true Lord our God, you are steadfast and incomprehensible; unchangeable, changing all things; invisible, seeing all things; immortal, without place, without end, uncircumscribed, nowhere bounded, ineffable, inestimable, unspeakable, unsearchable, unmoved, touching all things, past tracing out, to be feared and terrible, to be venerated and revered, to be honoured and dreaded, never new, never old, renewing all things, and bringing the proud into old age, and they do not know it: ever acting, ever at rest, gathering and not in need, bearing all things without burden, filling all things without being enclosed, creating and protecting all things, nourishing and perfecting [them], seeking though nothing is lacking to you. You love, and do not burn; you are jealous, and are untroubled; you repent, and do not grieve; you are angry, and are tranquil; you change your works, but never your counsel; you take back what you find, and you never lost [it]; never in want, and you rejoice in gains; never greedy, and you exact interest. More than is due is paid to you, so that you may be a debtor: and who has anything that is not yours? You pay debts, owing no one; you remit debts, losing nothing.

CHAPTER V. How God is far and near and whole in all things. You who alone give life to all things, who created all things; who are everywhere and everywhere whole, who can be felt and cannot be seen, who are nowhere absent, and yet are far from the thoughts of the wicked; who are not absent even there where you are far, since where you are not present by grace, you are present by punishment. You who touch all things, and yet do not touch all things equally. For some you touch that they may be, yet not that they may live and feel; some you touch that they may be, live and feel, yet not that they may discern; some you touch that they may be, live, feel and discern. And though you are never unlike yourself, yet you touch unlike things in unlike ways. You who are present everywhere, and can scarcely be found; whom, though you stand still, we follow, and are not able to lay hold of.

CHAPTER VI. That God touches all things, yet does not move. You who hold all things, fill all things, embrace all things, surpass all things, sustain all things; you do not sustain from one side and surpass from another, nor fill from one side and embrace from another; but by embracing you fill, and by filling you embrace; by sustaining you surpass, and by surpassing you sustain. You who teach the hearts of the faithful without the din of words, who reach from end to end mightily, and order all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1). You who are not stretched out by places, nor varied by times, nor have approach or withdrawal. You who dwell in light unapproachable, which no man has seen, nor can see (1 Tim. 6:16): abiding at rest in yourself, you go round the whole everywhere.

CHAPTER VII. That God is not divided into parts. For you cannot be cut or divided, since you are truly one; nor are you made into parts, but whole, holding the whole, you fill the whole, illumine the whole, possess the whole. This mystery the human mind cannot grasp or conceive, nor can an orator's tongue tell it, nor can the volumes of libraries of extended discourse unfold it. Though books should fill the whole world, your unutterable knowledge cannot be uttered. Since you are truly unspeakable, you can in no way be written or enclosed, you who are the fount of divine light and the sun of eternal brightness. For you are great without quantity, and therefore immeasurable; good without quality, therefore truly and supremely good; and no one is good but you alone.

CHAPTER VIII. That God's willing is doing. You whose will is deed, for whom to will is to be able; who made by will alone all the things you created out of nothing; who possess all your creation without any need, and govern without toil, and rule without weariness. And there is nothing that may disturb the order of your rule, either in the highest or in the lowest things. You who are held to be in all places without place, and contain all things without encompassing, and are present everywhere without position or motion. You who are not the author of evil, which you cannot do, you who can do all things; nor have you ever repented of having made anything, nor are you disturbed by the storm of any commotion of mind, nor is a particle of the whole earth your kingdom. You approve or command no shameful deeds or crimes. You never lie, since you are eternal truth: by whose goodness alone we were made, and by whose justice we pay penalties, and by whose clemency we are set free.

CHAPTER IX. That nothing is to be worshipped but God. For nothing heavenly, nothing earthly, nothing fiery, and nothing that the sense of the body reaches, is to be adored or worshipped in place of you, who truly are what you are, and are not changed: to whom above all and especially belongs that which the Greeks say, ὢν ["being"], the Latins Est ["is"]: since you are always the selfsame, and your years shall not fail (Ps. 101:28). Hence indeed it is plainly given to be understood that you, our God whom we worship, true and almighty God, are without doubt invisible, though you may be seen by a devout understanding; incomprehensible, though you may be represented through grace; inestimable, though you may be devoutly believed and holily thought of by human senses; ineffable, though you may be spoken of somehow, improperly, in the ordinary words of human speech: therefore [you are] true and so great. Moreover, whatever can be known, grasped, thought or said of you is less [than you]. But what is incomprehensible and immeasurable, unspeakable and infinite, is known to you alone. For this is what surpasses every sense; this too is what makes you to be esteemed, and believed for certain, and called the universal God, since you cannot be found out completely, since you cannot be understood or grasped whole: so the force of your greatness presents you to us as both known and unknown. And this is the sum of the guilt of those who scorn to know you, who refuse to serve you their Creator. They have what they may revere in knowing, they have what they may marvel at in not knowing: they have what to fear, they have what to love. For if you lay wholly open to our knowledge, you could by no means be believed the living and true God: so far were those who were thought gods found false, since who and of what kind and how great they were could be known in every respect.

CHAPTER X. That God made all things by the Word alone. But you, our wondrous and mighty God, who brought forth out of nothing the whole mass of this world with all its apparatus of elements, bodies and spirits, by the word with which you commanded, by the reason with which you ordered, by the power with which you were able, to adorn the majesty of your glory; who, bidding time go forth from eternity, and remaining stable, grant all things to be moved; who adorned the earth with manifold growth of fruits, and the sky with the fair light of the stars, whose names, signs, powers, courses and times you alone know. You gentle, you kind, strong, jealous and most unconquered Sabaoth, visiting the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, and showing mercy to thousands of thousands to those who love you (Exod. 20:5) and fear your name. If your works are so great and unsearchable, beautiful and astounding, let those who wish say how you, their most beautiful Creator, can be grasped. For it is clear that the maker of all things is far otherwise than the things he willed to be made by him. Yet from the beauty of circumscribed nature and the wondrous appearance of worldly things, your beauty, which you yourself are, since you are simple, and the excellence of your glory, which cannot be circumscribed, can to some degree be understood, although no sense can reach the infinite and incomprehensible greatness of your divinity, not even that of those heavenly citizens: yet in a wondrous way your essence is known, while it is believed to be.

CHAPTER XI. On the two syllables of God. Whenever I recall or hear the two short syllables and four letters with which Deus [God] is written (for this name is rightly due to you alone, Almighty), and when I behold the mighty works of your power and the wondrous creation of the world, that is, consider the beauty of the cosmopoeia [world-making], and at the same time silently ponder within myself your mercies which have been from of old (let those who wish marvel at your power, but I am more astonished noting your mercies): surely in these four letters and two short syllables I contemplate, with the gaze of the mind and the sincere eyes of faith, something infinite and incomprehensible, immeasurable and unutterable, according to the knowledge and ability you deign to grant to me, so small a man. For are you, our God, two short syllables, or do we adore two short syllables, or desire to come to two short syllables, which almost cease to sound before they begin, and in which there is no room for the second unless the first has first passed away? Rather there abides something great, and it is greatly and supremely so, incomparable and most excellent of all, which is called God, although the sound does not abide when "God" is said.

CHAPTER XII. That God is not seen in his own nature. But since the flesh does not know the spirit, and invisible things are not seen by visible ones (for we walk by faith, and not by sight), you, our God, exceedingly good and merciful, taking thought for human weakness, deign to make yourself known to us, not by what is proper to you, but by some other likeness. Hence you are even described as having the character of our members, willing that things unworthy of suffering be said of you yourself for this purpose: that, since we cannot know you as you are in this present misery, you may draw us through what is ours to what is yours, and that we, while you condescend to us, may more easily rise up to you.

CHAPTER XIII. On the image of God made in man. Indeed in many ways, to signify yourself to men, you draw likenesses from lower things to yourself, you who, it is agreed, are in truth, according to your own nature, invisible and incorporeal, incomprehensible and uncircumscribed; and therefore we believe that you have never appeared to anyone according to your essence, but in the ways you willed, through an assumed appearance of creatures, for the bringing about of [your] purposes. So the followers of the heresy of the Anthropomorphites are deceived, who, when they read that man was made in the image and likeness of God, assert with foolish rashness that you have a human form, whereas in that place you are said, or believed, to have created the mind, not the flesh, in your image.

CHAPTER XIV. On the breadth, length, height and depth of God. Truly, human speech says nothing worthy of you, for nothing is worthily said of you according to quality or quantity, position or state or motion. And yet breadth, length, height and depth are read to be in you in a certain way. But [there is] the breadth of love, by which you gather us from error and hold us in the truth; the length, by which you patiently bear with us in our wickedness, until you restore us, amended, to the homeland to come; the height, by which you surpass every sense of both men and angels by the immensity of your knowledge; the depth also, by which you set those to be damned below according to equity, and as a just judge foreordain [them] by right judgement. Let him, therefore, who wishes to have some foretaste of what is proper to you, supreme and good Deity, pass beyond every creature and direct the gaze of his mind beyond all things.

CHAPTER XV. On the knowledge of the Holy Trinity. For then a man, placed far from vanity, is held more fully in the truth, when, all other things being removed from his peaceful gaze, God, who is whatever is in his heart, is piously believed and holily thought upon. But although there is no one who in this vale of tears can effectually grasp or define you, yet something great and very wonderful has been given to our age: to know of you, the supreme good, your grace indeed revealing it to us. Who before us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come (1 Cor. 10:11), could hear or know such things so plainly about the Trinity and the unity, about the persons and the substance? Of you, God the Father, that you are from no one, and therefore are called unbegotten; of your Son, that he is begotten and is from you, not from himself; of the Holy Spirit too, that he is proceeding and is not from himself, but from you and the Son, whose Spirit he is. So much so that, as you the Father can be called neither begotten nor proceeding, so the Son [is] neither unbegotten nor proceeding, so neither should the Holy Spirit be called unbegotten nor begotten: so that the property of the persons may plainly show us you, one Father, together with one Son and one Holy Spirit. Who in earlier ages, believing in you as one God and confessing you as threefold, neither separating the substance nor confounding the persons, so wisely understood, so openly perceived, so truly knew? Your Son indeed, sent out into our public view from your bosom, has more clearly disclosed this rule of right faith to this last age. Before you showed the Creator to the creature, you were known, God, in Judaea alone, and in Israel the great fame and worship of your name was heard (Ps. 75:2). But was it so clearly, or as much as among us who are placed under grace? Of the undivided Trinity very few then perceived anything at all. For the sons of the lawgivers, struck with a deserved blindness, are still ignorant of what they ought to know of the one Trinity, or the threefold unity: wretched men, refusing to confess anything besides one God, and chattering against us with malicious words when we say that you, the Father, have a Son. But how many and how true are the things it has been given to us who came from the Gentiles to know of the God threefold and one, is proved by the hearts that believe, and also by the mouths that confess, and no less by the very scourgings and the death which were inflicted for this very confession: for it is written, I have understood more than the elders (Ps. 118:100).

CHAPTER XVI. That the Trinity is undivided. To create belongs to God alone. How the Word is in the Father. Lord our God, living and true, if you were not a Trinity, it would not have been said by the voice of Truth: Go, baptise all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matt. 28:19). For we would not be commanded, Lord God, to be baptised in the name of one who was not the Lord God. And again, if you, the Trinity, were not one God, it would by no means have been said by your voice: Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God (Deut. 6:4). So if you were not yourself God the Father, and your Son, your Word, Jesus Christ, were not himself [God], and your gift were not himself the Holy Spirit, we would not read in the Writings of truth, God sent his Son (Gal. 4:4). Nor would you, Only-begotten, say of the Holy Spirit, Whom the Father will send in my name (John 14:26), and, Whom I will send you from the Father (John 15:26); and elsewhere, I and the Father are one (John 10:30); and, Whoever sees me sees the Father also. For I am in the Father, and the Father is in me; and, The Father abiding in me himself does the works (John 14:9, 10). For by these words what else do you lead us to believe, except God threefold and one, you the teacher of truth, in whose breast are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge? You also say, My teaching is not mine (John 7:16); and, The word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father's who sent me (John 14:24). A wonderful thing, a thing to be marvelled at! Speak then, speak, Word of the Father; answer, I beg, Power and Wisdom of the supreme Beginning; but you yourself are beginning from beginning, yet not two beginnings, but surely one beginning. Speak, Word ever abiding, teach your servant who humbly asks. For what is so much yours as you? But you are yours and not yours, since you are not from yourself, as you often testify in many places, but from the Father, whose word you are, not sounding through syllables and fleeting, but ever living and abiding unmoved. And therefore a word, not one that ceases when uttered, but one that remains when born; not transitory, but eternal; not made, but begotten; and not only begotten, but only-begotten; to whom reason is present as he orders [things], and power is at hand as he accomplishes [them], as being true God and supreme Lord. For the Father begot you, the only-begotten Word, from himself, through whom he created all things from nothing. And therefore we believe without doubt that, if you were not the all-knowing and all-powerful Word, God, all things would by no means have been made through you. How can a creature create anything? Surely God alone, who is not created, is able to create: for nothing except God is uncreated. Far be it from our understanding to confess that anything is born of the Father except the Son; and therefore nothing but God could be born of God.

Hence, Word of the Father, when I wish to consider you, no words suffice by which I might be able to unfold you. And when shall I be able to speak fully or worthily? Who, about whom? Man about God, the work about the maker, the creature about the Creator, the small about the immeasurable, the temporal about the eternal: whose venerable power is most almighty, by which you made us out of free goodness; yet no less venerable is the grace by which you saved us with most almighty mercy. You who both made freely the work of creating omnipotence and fulfilled almightily the work of saving grace, having indeed perpetual power both to found what was unfounded and to restore what was lost. Nor, then, would that foremost of theologians, who contemplated the highest things more deeply than the rest with eagle's gaze, have poured forth in writing, In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: he was in the beginning with God (John 1:1, 2), unless you, God the Word, were always with the Father, always together with the Father, always from the Father, always in the Father: not as a vessel in a vessel, or a town beside a city, but as wisdom within the wise, truth in the truthful, goodness in the good, eternity in the eternal: for nothing else can be in the substance of the Father except God, equal and coeternal with him by whom you were begotten. Let all heretical depravity therefore be struck dumb and perish with its authors, which with ever-hostile strife now divides the substance, now confounds the persons. May mother Church grow, I pray, in faith, and be made more and more fruitful in pious deeds, she who judges it profane and exceedingly impious to worship three gods, [or] not to distinguish the Trinity in persons. She, in short, instructed in heavenly disciplines, believes, confesses and teaches without any doubt one substance and three persons, knowing all things that belong to the rule of faith. Taught from boyhood by her teaching and heaven-inspired doctrine, I believe with the heart, I confess with the mouth you, O supreme Trinity, one power and undivided majesty.

CHAPTER XVII. On the knowledge of the incorporeal divine essence. I confess you, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, threefold in persons, one in substance, the true God almighty, maker of things visible and invisible: not a body or placed in a body, nor mixed together from different kinds, nor shaped by a framework of limbs, but of one simple and incorporeal, invisible and uncircumscribed nature. I believe and confess you, the true Father, the source of supreme goodness and of the whole deity, God of uncircumscribed and unbegotten majesty, taking your beginning from nothing but giving beginning to all things, begetting the Son not by bodily offspring nor from outside, not by necessity nor by will, but by nature.

I confess you also, the true Son, born ineffably of the Father without beginning, true God only-begotten, through whom all things were made, and the true Word of the Father, not made, not created, not adoptive, but begotten and of one substance with the Father, and so equal in all things to God the Father that you cannot be inferior either in time, or in rank, or in power. And I confess that you are as great as he of whom you were begotten, as great as he himself is who begot you. But because I say that the Son is begotten of the Father, I do not ascribe any time to the divine and ineffable generation; nor do I say that the Father ever began, nor you his Son. Since he was always Father, you were therefore never not Son. For we cannot confess the Father eternal otherwise than by confessing the Son also coeternal. For a father is so called from a son; and since he was always Father, there is no doubt that he always had a Son.

CHAPTER XVIII. On the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son. I believe you also, the Holy Spirit, to be true God, not made, nor created, nor begotten, nor unbegotten, but proceeding indescribably from the Father and the Son, and abiding substantially in the Father and at the same time in the Son. So, then, you proceed from both in such a way that you remain inseparably in both; and [you are] so equal in all things to God the Father and the Son, coeternal, consubstantial, that you cannot differ from, or be cut off from, those from whom you proceed, either in power, or in will, or in eternity, or in substance. Therefore the eternal Father without birth, the eternal Son with birth, the eternal Holy Spirit with procession without birth; the whole Father abiding in the Son and the Holy Spirit, the whole Son in the Father and the Holy Spirit, the whole Holy Spirit in the Father and the Son; and the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God almighty, reigning with one power and one kingdom, one majesty, one eternity, from then and now and always everywhere: [this] I believe with the heart, confess with the mouth, and love with the mind.

Directing my intention to this rule of faith, as far as you have made me able, my God, I have sought you, and have desired to see with the understanding what I have believed. For the sake of this I entered the storehouse of the many delights on which mother Church is fed; there I considered a great many things, and began to examine them one by one. And while I ran anxiously and eagerly here and there, you, being good and wishing to help the desire which you gave, sent forth the hand of your mercy and loosed the knot of my uncertainty; and therefore it delights me greatly to think about you, to speak about you, and to bring forth your praises with a longing heart according to the measure of my smallness, so that in the present misery I may be held, Lord, only in body, but with you in mind and with all eagerness.

CHAPTER XIX. On the comparison of the three persons. How venerable are the mysteries of the Trinity and of the Eucharist. God threefold and one, kindle in me the light of knowledge, by which I may deserve to understand you, God threefold and one, as you are God threefold and one. And remove from me more and more, as you have begun, the darkness of ignorance, so that I may see spiritual things spiritually, as far as is possible for human frailty. Give me understanding on this way on which I walk with you as guide, and inspire me, and always teach me through your grace how one ought to believe in you blamelessly, so that I may know you as one God in essence and, incomprehensibly, as threefold in persons: the Father unbegotten, the Only-begotten from the Father, the Holy Spirit proceeding from both and remaining in both; [that] no moment of priority or posteriority intervenes among the three, nor do they have a divided rule; nor in creating [is there] divided counsel, nor in ruling and perfecting creatures divided help and work. Whatever is of nature there is unbroken; whatever is of person is unconfused. O ineffable mystery, and difficult beyond others for the understanding! The other sacraments which are held in your Church, Lord, are wonderful and venerable; but this sacrament of yours surpasses them all. This mystery of your undivided Trinity, and that Sacrament of the heavenly table which feeds faithful and pious souls with flesh and gives them blood to drink, so that they may not hunger nor thirst for ever, make me, my God, with a pure and simple conscience, to perceive and believe, to receive and retain, especially among all others. Do not allow, I beg, Lord, my faith in them to waver in any way; but grant me of your mercy always so to believe and understand in them and concerning them as their truth is. Let your grace enter into my heart, which sounds without sound and without noise; let it speak there all the truth of such great mysteries; let that teacher of virtues and judge of all truths flood my soul with light and sweetness everywhere within and on every side without; and so, by shining upon it and giving it savour, let it establish and confirm it in the very centre of truth, so that I may neither wish nor be able to think otherwise about such great mysteries than as is fitting and right. Almighty goodness, whose ears of mercy are open to the very desires of your poor, understand the cry of my heart, and favour my prayers. Grant, Lord, that with the very palate of the mind I may perceive, taste and savour these ineffable sacraments: for they are great and exceedingly wonderful, and I, a little one, fail in contemplating them whenever I raise the eyes of faith to look upon them. But since both are equally necessary to us for salvation, God, author of all things, invisible creator, who are in substance the supreme and one Godhead, and in persons the true and perfect Trinity: I entreat you, God the Father, from whom are all things, and your Son, through whom are all things, and together the Holy Spirit, in whom are all things; you, my Lord, whom I confess as one and true God in trinity, by whom we have been created, set free and enlightened, I humbly ask, eager for such great mysteries: give me milk, nourish me, and stretch out my smallness to the measure of the age of the perfect man, so that I may be able to take this solid and perfect food. For your eyes have seen my imperfection (Ps. 133:16).

CHAPTER XX. That the divine substance is undivided. God the Father, giver of all good things, to whom supplication is never made without hope of mercy, with your Son and the Holy Spirit, give what my soul desires of you and asks of you. For of those whose substance is one, the gift too is one, the working one, the bestowal one, and the power one; so that, according to a deeper understanding, a certain unity may be perceived even in the very property of the persons. Indeed, the inseparable unity of your nature cannot have separable persons: for just as you are trinity in unity and unity in trinity, so you cannot have a separation of persons. Those persons are indeed sometimes named singly; but you, God the Trinity, have willed to show yourself inseparable in persons in such a way that there is no name for you in any person which is not referred to another person according to the rule of relation; as the Father is most truly referred to the Son, and the Son to the Father, or the Holy Spirit to the Father and the Son. But those names which signify your substance or power or essence, or whatever is properly said of God, befit all the persons equally, such as God, great, good, eternal, almighty, and all things that are said by nature of you, God. There is therefore no name of nature which can befit you, God the Father, in such a way that it cannot befit your Son or the Holy Spirit. We say that you, God the Father, are by nature God; but the Son too is by nature God, and the Holy Spirit too is by nature God; yet not three gods, but one God, Father and Son and Holy Spirit. Therefore, holy Trinity, God, you are to be understood in sense as inseparable in persons, although in utterance you have separable names; because you in no way admit the plural number in names of nature. For in this it is shown that the persons cannot be divided in the holy Trinity, which is the one true God: that the name of any person always looks to another person. If I say Father, I point to the Son; if I name the Son, I proclaim the Father; if I call on the Holy Spirit, it must be understood that he is the spirit of someone, that is, of the Father and the Son. But you, unity of deity, manifold in the plurality of persons, are numerably innumerable, and therefore measurably immeasurable, and weighably unweighable: for we do not profess [anything other than] the supreme goodness, which you yourself are, [as] the origin from which are all things, through which are all things, in which are all things; but by participation in it we call all things good.

CHAPTER XXI. That in the Godhead there is no matter. For your divine substance has always been and is without matter, though it is not without form; and while you press this form like a seal upon each single thing, you without doubt make them differ from you, with no change in you by increase or loss. Whatever is in the nature of created things is your creature, O threefold unity and one trinity, God, whose omnipotence governs, rules and fills all the things which it created. Nor do we say that you fill all things in such a way that they contain you, but rather that they are contained by you.

CHAPTER XXII. That there is no part in God, nor division. Nor do you fill all things part by part, nor is it in any way to be thought that each thing receives you according to the size of its portion, that is, the greatest more and the least less; rather you yourself are whole in all things, or all things are in you. Your omnipotence encloses all things, and no one will be able to find a way in to the power of escaping it. For whoever does not have you appeased will by no means escape you angered. For the immensity of your divine greatness is this: that we understand you to be within all things, but not enclosed; outside all things, but not shut out.

CHAPTER XXIII. That God contains all things. And so you are inner, so that you contain all things; you are outer, so that by the immensity of your uncircumscribed greatness you rule all things by enclosing them. By the fact that you are outer, then, you are shown to be the creator; by the fact that you are inner, you are shown to govern and rule all things. And so that the things which have been created should not be without you, you are within all things; but so that they should not be outside you, you are outer, so that all things are enclosed by you, not by spatial greatness but by the presence of power, because you are present everywhere and all things are present to you, although some understand this and some do not understand it.

CHAPTER XXIV. That the Godhead is not bodily. These things and many others mother Church has taught me, the holy mother, universal and orthodox, of which you willed me to become a member through your grace; and by her heavenly teaching you have deigned, Lord, in your mercy, to make me so certain and secure in all things, through the constant illumination of your inspiration, as if I were gazing on many things which lie hidden, closed in mysteries, not through a mirror but face to face. She taught, then, that you, the only living and true God, are not bodily, nor capable of suffering, nor touchable; that no part of you can be perceived by bodily eyes; that nothing of your substance and nature is in any way violable, or compounded, or fashioned, or greater or lesser; but in every way and on every side perfect without deformity, great without quantity, good without quality, everlasting without time, life without death, strong without weakness, truth without falsehood, whole everywhere without place, present everywhere without position, filling all things without extension, meeting all things everywhere without contraction, surpassing all things without motion, remaining within all things without standing still, creating all things without need, ruling all things without toil, giving a beginning to all things without beginning of your own, making all things changeable without change of your own, and reigning always and everywhere, remaining without end. Lord, one God, Trinity, God, who surpass all things beyond comparison: you are so ineffable, infinite and incomprehensible that everything which can be said of you is very small indeed. For we say many things, but we cannot fully say what you are. And since you yourself are the consummation of all words, when we have come to you, these many things which we say will without doubt cease, and you will remain one, all in all, and without end we shall say all things as one, praising you, the one, and ourselves made one in you: seeing you continually without end, the incorporeal and by nature unchangeable trinity, and knowing all things in you, and having in you joy that will remain forever, healed of every weakness, as transformed into that glory of immortality.

CHAPTER XXV. On the vision of God. One Trinity. When this vision comes which is promised to be given face to face, when all mysteries will be openly proclaimed, and sight will succeed faith and the thing itself hope, then, knowing more clearly and certainly, we shall behold that there is nothing created or subservient in you, one Trinity, nothing unequal, nothing equal [only] by grace, nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or less, nothing foreign or serving another, nothing inserted by persuasion or by stealth, nothing differing in character or will, nothing singular in function or communicable to another, nothing confused, all perfect; because all is in one and one in all, yet not solitary: since in you and with you we worship and adore you, holy Father, the highest good and highest wisdom and highest kindness, the one beginning of all things; and your Truth, through which we understand you, in no part unlike you, which is the form of all things and which alone fulfils what all things desire; and together the very Gift of both, by which all things that are blessed are blessed, namely the one unchangeable Trinity.

CHAPTER XXVI. An example from fire and the soul. For when what is one is repeated a third time, a number is not piled up, but it is asserted that it is one. Begetting, begotten, and proceeding: three persons, but one substance. As fire, brightness, heat are three names but one thing, so memory, understanding, will, but one soul; they are shown inseparably and they act inseparably. If this is found in creatures, what is to be understood of you, the Creator? For the nature of your Godhead is in every way immovable and unchangeable; but the persons are movable according to relation, not according to property; and so there is trinity in the relation of the persons, but unity in the substance of the nature: unity because of the inseparable essence of the deity, trinity because of the diversity of the names. For we confess not only names but also the properties of the names, that is, persons, or, as the Greeks express it, ὑποστάσεις, that is, substances.

CHAPTER XXVII. On the unchangeableness of God. The incomprehensible mystery of the Trinity. Yet we say these things about you, our God, as human understanding is able to grasp them. But who, set in this life, even with a breast clear as crystal, would be able to penetrate the inner mysteries of your Trinity itself: how Father, Son and Holy Spirit, you are three persons and one nature; how, while you, Father, are called unbegotten and the Son begotten, the Holy Spirit is said to be neither begotten nor unbegotten but proceeding; how the Son is born of you, the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from you and the Son; how the Son by being born does not proceed, and the Holy Spirit by proceeding is not born; how the Son is not from himself but from you, and yet is not later than you from whom he is; how the Holy Spirit proceeds from you and the Son, and yet is not preceded by you from whom he proceeds; how you three are one, and one three; how in relation to one another you are three, in essence one; how, threefold and one God, you are not in a place but everywhere; and you are not everywhere part by part, but everywhere whole, everywhere present without position and place and motion? Who, I ask, could consider these things? Who could comprehend them, however endowed with goodness or knowledge? Yet this is laid up in the hope of the promise, that we shall see you, Lord; and each one the more clearly, the more purely he has lived here. For the pure in heart, as Scripture testifies, shall see God (Matt. 5:8). For when all the darkness of the mind has been wiped away, it will be seen openly how the Son, who is by arising, is not subsequent to you, O Father, from whom he arises; and how the Spirit of both, who is brought forth by procession, is not preceded by you who bring him forth; how you are both one divisibly three and three indivisibly one. For the brightness, once seen, will seize and lift up the pure gaze of the loving mind to the beauty of your majesty not yet laid open to us. But that brightness is the nature, and that nature is the brightness. This vision indeed is now begun by faith, but will then be perfected in sight, when we shall drink at the very fountain the Wisdom coeternal with you, which we now receive through the mouths of teachers. And all the sacraments and all secrets will then appear to us, not by the words of teachers (for we shall need no mysteries when we see you face to face), but from there, unless I am mistaken, from where the angels see you. What will be able to be hidden from us then, when you, our God, life of the living, cause of causes, form of forms, most beautiful form, unformed form, make yourself known to us in clear vision?

CHAPTER XXVIII. That the Godhead lacks matter. For it does not seem unworthy of you when we call you form. For your essence can be called both beauty and form (not in vain are both 'most beauteous' and 'most shapely' set down in your praise); but a form which lacks matter and motion, time and place, and therefore is one, and is that which it is; but other things are not that which they are. This alone can most truly say, I am who am (Exod. 3:14). This form is so great and of such a kind that the human mind dares to claim nothing for itself in this life from the vision of its beauty, which you reserve as a reward solely for your elect in the recompense to come.

CHAPTER XXIX. On thirst without need. The blessed see God unequally. When, therefore, we have come to you, the fountain of life, the eternal light and the sweetest beauty, from the vision of you there will be delightfully impressed upon us thirst and at the same time fullness. But need will be far from the thirst, and loathing far from the fullness, because thirsting we shall be filled, and filled we shall thirst. In short, you will be our eternal life, joy and crown. The blessed vision of you will be the reward of our labour, so that after the darkness of this mortality we may rejoice, kindled by the light of your glory. And so we shall see the unchangeableness of your essence, so that through it we too may be made unchangeable, but not as you see [yourself]. For in ourselves, whatever we shall be, we shall be able to know; but in you, who cannot be comprehended in what you are, whatever that is, when can we know it? And even if we shall be able to, we cannot yet; and yet when we shall be able, shall we be able to know you as you know yourself, O God? Even the rational and elect creature will not possess the vision of you equally; for each [will have it] according to the reward of his labour, but what is given to each to behold will fully suffice him. How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord (Ps. 30:20)! Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord (Ps. 83:5). Happy are those who have already crossed the sea of this mortality and have come to the harbour of everlasting security. Unhappy are we, who are still tossed on the open sea of this life by the storms surrounding us, and amid many dangers and various chances, uncertain, toilingly drag our ship along.

CHAPTER XXX. On eternal life. O Lord, grant us, with you as helmsman and guide, so to hold our course between Scylla and Charybdis that with our ship unharmed and our cargo safe we may come to you, the safest harbour. Happy the soul which, already joined to the blessed spirits, stands before your majesty, which [beholds] you, the uncircumscribed, which rejoices in the gift of everlasting incorruption. O living life, sweet and lovable, and ever to be remembered, where there is no enemy attacking, where there is no enticement, but the highest and certain security, and secure tranquillity, and tranquil gladness, and glad happiness, and happy eternity, and eternal blessedness, and the blessed vision and praise of you without end, O God! Would that this might come to pass, and this mortal body be clothed with immortality! Would that this life might cease and be ended as quickly as may be, a doubtful life, a blind life, a wretched life, which humours swell, pains waste away, fevers dry up, airs make sick, foods puff up, fasts emaciate, jests unloose, sorrows consume, anxiety constricts, security dulls, riches make boastful, poverty casts down, youth exalts, old age bends over, infirmity breaks, grief depresses; and after all these, death destroys, putting an end to all joys, so that when they have ceased to be, they are not even thought to have been. Now, now let it come, Lord, let it fly here, I beseech you, that kingdom which lacks death and is free of end, to which no times succeed through the ages, where continual day without night knows no time, where are those hymn-singing choirs of angels and the fellowship of the citizens on high, where is the sweet festival of those returning from the sad toil of this pilgrimage, where are the foreseeing choirs of the prophets, where is the judging number of the apostles, where is the victorious army of innumerable martyrs, and with them the constancy of the confessors, consoled by receiving its reward, where are faithful men whom the pleasure of this world could not soften from the strength of their manhood, and likewise holy women, who overcame their sex together with the world; where are boys who, while they were in the flesh, surpassed their years by their conduct, and old men whom age made weak, yet whom the strength of good works did not abandon. To the holy company of all these, and to the joy, enduring without end, of beholding your beauty, make me, Lord God, strive with my whole heart, run manfully, and arrive happily. Meanwhile, while [I am] in this maimed body, you who instil what is good, exercise my mind always in these meditations. Cleanse, then, the gaze of my heart, sharpen the understanding of my mind, kindle my spirit with heavenly fire, so that I may think of you alone, love you alone, have you alone in heart and on lips, you who are our reward to come without end. And so that I may bear the weight of my mortality more lightly, give light in my heart, give the word on my lips, open the secrets of the holy Scriptures, and give my inmost parts to drink of the depths of the mysteries of your kingdom. Give tears from love of you, give the wings of faith and the virtues, clothed with which I may fly up to you, and, hating the earth, seek heaven. This faith I confess through you, about you, in you, O blessed and blest and glorious Trinity, O true and highest and everlasting unity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, God, Lord, Paraclete; love, grace, communion; true light, light from light, true illumination; living life, life from the living, giver of life to the living; fountain, river, watering; one from himself, one from one, one from both; from one all things, through one all things, in one all things; that is, the Father from himself, the Son from the other, that is, from the Father, the Holy Spirit from both, that is, from the Father and the Son: Being from himself, Being from the other, Being from both; and the whole Being always in the three, and the whole Being equally in each; truthful Begetter, Truth begotten, the Holy Spirit the love of both. One power, equal majesty, like glory, one and the same essence. Wise Begetter, Wisdom begotten, and the Holy Spirit love.

CHAPTER XXXI. On the divine light. O God three and one, God almighty, with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration (James 1:17), and therefore with you the course of time is in no way varied by the alternation of day and night. O God, true light, who without approaching illuminate the things you choose, and without withdrawing abandon the things you reject; and therefore in you there comes no failing, no changeableness. O God, who, remaining unchangeable in yourself, so founded transitory things in themselves that with you they can in no way pass away; and therefore in your sight time does not flow away, which with us runs down to its end. O God, in whose eternity those things remain fixed which, not fixed, flow outward in the rolling of the ages; and therefore your eternity is one day, which is neither closed by an end nor opened by a beginning.

CHAPTER XXXII. That God is unchangeable. O God, who without change in yourself behold all things at once, and without stretching comprehend both the good which you help and the evil which you judge, both what in helping you reward and what in judging you condemn, you are not diverse in the things you dispose in diverse order. O God, who surround your works outside and fill them within, cover them above and bear them beneath; and though you are higher by power, lower by sustaining, outer by greatness, inner by subtlety, yet you are higher and lower without place, wide without breadth, subtle without thinning, and therefore you are nowhere by bulk of body, but by uncircumscribed substance and the immensity of unchangeable nature you are nowhere absent. But because you, the Creator, are far distant from [the creature], are you not contained in place? [You are] altogether [not] in place. You yourself are believed to be your own placeless place, an uncircumscribed spirit; whence it is hard to find where you are, but much harder where you are not. Who can subsist or be without you? And yet not all can be with you. For all things are from you, and subsist through you.

CHAPTER XXXIII. On the infinity of God. Thanks are given to God. The aim of this little book. O God, true and infinite blessedness, from whom and through whom and in whom all things are blessed that are blessed. O God, true and highest life, from whom and through whom and in whom all things live that truly and supremely live. O God, the good and the beautiful, from whom and through whom and in whom all things are good and beautiful that are good and truly beautiful. O God, above whom nothing, outside whom nothing, without whom nothing, beyond whom nothing, beneath whom nothing. O God, under whom the whole, with whom the whole, in whom the whole. O God, from whom all things, through whom all things, in whom all things. O God, to whom faith rouses us, hope raises us, love joins us. O God, who bid us ask, and make us find, and open to those who knock (Matt. 7:7). O God, to turn away from whom is to fall, to turn to whom is to rise again, to remain in whom is to stand firm. O God, whom no one loses unless deceived, no one seeks unless prompted, no one finds unless pure or purified. O God, by the help of whose kindness the subject serves well and the superior rules well; and therefore without you none of them walks the right path or rules in right order. O God invisible and immense, ineffable and eternal, incomprehensible and incorporeal, immortal and perpetual, unchangeable and uncircumscribed, wonderful and blessed, unspeakable, for whom to be is to live, and to be wise and to understand, to know and to be able, to be beautiful and to be bright are one and the same; because you are simple and cannot be divided. You are my God, living and true, kind God, my great king. You, one God, I worship, the one principle of natures, by whom the universe is begun and perfected and held together: one God from whom we are, through whom we are, in whom we are, from whom we departed, to whom we became unlike; the principle to which we return, and the form which we follow, and the grace by which we are reconciled; the one by whose authorship we were made, and the peace by which we cleave to unity; one God by whom as creator we live, loving whom and enjoying whom we live blessedly; you I praise, bless and adore, I give thanks to your clemency and goodness for all your gifts and bestowals, and for all the benefits of your mercy which you lavish on my soul and body, and have always lavished from my boyhood and my cradle, for your own sake and your holy name's. Whence I have learned by experience that you, our God, are a God of infinite mercy, immense majesty and freely given kindness: who wonderfully direct and guard your servants amid adversity and prosperity, and so govern their life on either side that adversity succeeds prosperity and prosperity succeeds adversity. Let all your works, then, confess to you, Lord, and let your saints bless you (Ps. 144:10); and that by confessing they may come to their senses, let even sinners themselves not cease from your praises. Though I, one of them, am more prone to sins, yet with a longing heart I sing your praises; if not with the praise or worthiness I owe, I do it with what ability I have. Look, I pray, with serene face upon this service of my littleness, and with gracious condescension accept this tiny sacrifice of the confession of my faith, so that what came from you may return to you; looking not so much to what I devoutly offer as to what I have most devoutly wished and wish to say. For whatever is unfitting or offends you, my soul abhors. Would that I could [sing] such things as those hymn-singing choirs of angels! O how diligently would I pour myself out wholly in your praises, and splendidly, unwearied, proclaim the song of your glory in the midst of the Church! But because I cannot as they do, shall I be wholly silent? Woe, Lord, to those who are silent about you, who loosen the mouths of the dumb and make the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisd. 10:21). But since little ones may at least stammer your praises, accept, I pray, the sacrifice from the hand of my tongue, from the love of my heart.

But forgive, I ask, Lord, your most unworthy and unhappy servant who speaks with you about you at such length. Forgive, O merciful one, for it was not in rash presumption but in eager longing for you that I gave my effort to this little gathering of flowers: so that I might always have with me a short and handy word about you, by whose reading, whenever I grow lukewarm, I may be rekindled into love of you. For we are set in the midst of snares, and therefore we need a constant reminder, by which, roused, we may run back to you, our true and highest good, when we slip away. There are, indeed, many contemplations by which the devout soul is exercised and advances towards you; but none of them so delights me, or so holds my mind's attention, as that which treats of what is proper to you. Therefore I thought it necessary to pluck out for myself this little discourse alone, in which, concerning the omnipotence of your majesty, as I believe with the heart unto justice, so I confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10): you, God the Father unbegotten, you the only-begotten Son, you the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, the holy and undivided Trinity, one God, infinite in greatness, almighty in power, highest in goodness, inestimable in wisdom, terrible in counsels, just in judgements, most secret in thoughts, truthful in words, holy in works, abundant in mercies; most patient towards those who sin, most loving towards those who repent; ever the selfsame, eternal and everlasting, immortal and unchangeable; whom no spaces widen, no smallness of places narrows, no receptacles confine; whom will does not vary, necessity does not corrupt, sad things do not disturb, glad things do not soothe; from whom forgetting takes nothing away and to whom remembering gives nothing back, for whom past things do not pass and future things do not come after; to whom origin gives no beginning, times no increase, and chance will give no end: but before the ages, and in the ages, and through the ages you live for ever; and to you be perpetual praise and eternal glory, highest power and singular honour, perpetual kingdom and dominion without end, through the infinite, unwearied and immortal ages of ages. Amen.
